hints: Start from $\mu = (e/m)\tau$ and list what each symbol means here: $e$ is electron charge, $m$ is electron mass and $\tau$ is a time between collisions.
Recall the SI base units for those three quantities: mass is $\text{kg}$ and time $\tau$ is $\text{s}$, but charge is not a base unit since $1 \text{ C} = 1 \text{ A s}$.
Multiply the units as $(\text{charge unit} / \text{kg}) \times \text{s}$ and collect the powers of $\text{A}$, $\text{s}$ and $\text{kg}$ to compare with options A to D.
walkthrough: Identify the given relation $\mu = \left(e/m\right) \tau$, so the unit of $\mu$ is (unit of $e$ divided by unit of $m$) multiplied by unit of $\tau$.
State the SI base units: charge $e$ is measured in coulombs, where $1 \text{ C} = 1 \text{ A s}$, so in base units $e$ is $\text{A s}$.
State the other base units: mass $m$ is $\text{kg}$ and collision time $\tau$ is $\text{s}$.
Substitute units into the equation: unit of $\mu = (\text{A s} / \text{kg}) \times \text{s} = \text{A s}^2 \text{kg}^{-1}$.
Check the result uses only base units $\text{A}$, $\text{s}$ and $\text{kg}$ with correct powers, matching the form with $\text{s}^2$ in the numerator. This is option B.

options.A: This omits one power of time because it uses $e$ as $\text{A}$ instead of $\text{A s}$ and so misses the $\tau$ factor.
options.B: Combining $e$ in $\text{A s}$, $m$ in $\text{kg}$ and $\tau$ in $\text{s}$ gives $\text{A s}^2 \text{kg}^{-1}$.
options.C: This has only $\text{s}^1$ because it counts the charge $e$ or the time $\tau$ but not both time contributions.
options.D: This has $\text{s}^{-2}$ which would come from dividing by time squared rather than multiplying by $e$ and $\tau$.
